Leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC for an INLAvanilla fit

Source: R/loo.R
loo.Rd

loo() estimates how well the model predicts new data by leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO), and waic() by the widely applicable information criterion. Both work from the fit alone, with no refitting and no posterior draws, by a second-order Taylor expansion of each unit's log-likelihood (Alhyari et al., 2026), as in INLAvaan.

Both need the log-likelihood split into one term per observation, or per independent unit, which inla_vanilla() never sees. You supply it as loglik: write the log-likelihood terms and the log-prior as separate functions, and logpost as their sum.

Usage

loo(object, ...)

waic(object, ...)

# Default S3 method
loo(object, ...)

# Default S3 method
waic(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'inla_vanilla'
loo(object, loglik, ...)

# S3 method for class 'inla_vanilla'
waic(object, loglik, ...)

Arguments

object

An object of class inla_vanilla.

...

Further arguments passed to loglik, such as the data. As in stats::optim(), a name that abbreviates object or loglik (such as l) would be taken as that argument, so give such data a longer name. If the loo package is attached after inlavanilla, its generics loo(x, ...) and waic(x, ...) are the ones called, and they take an argument named x as the fit: then do not name data x, or call inlavanilla::loo().

loglik

A function loglik(theta, ...) returning the log-likelihood terms, one per observation or independent unit, at the named parameter vector theta (on the scale of logpost). Their sum plus the log-prior is logpost. Names, if any, label the units.

Value

loo() returns an object of class inla_vanilla_loo, which also has class loo: a list with

  • estimates: a matrix with rows elpd_loo, p_loo and looic and columns Estimate and SE;

  • pointwise: a matrix with one row per unit and columns elpd_loo (the log CPO), p_loo, looic and k (the unit's largest leverage);

  • order: the order of the expansion used, 2 or 1;

  • first_order_units: the units whose second-order term does not exist, if any;

  • theta: the point of the expansion, and calls: the number of calls of loglik;

  • warnings: the messages of any warnings raised.

waic() returns an object of class inla_vanilla_waic (also waic and loo) with the same layout, with rows and columns elpd_waic, p_waic and waic.

Details

Write \(\ell_u(\vartheta) = \log p(y_u \mid \vartheta)\) for the log-likelihood of unit \(u\). The leave-one-out predictive density of unit \(u\), its conditional predictive ordinate, is $$\mathrm{CPO}_u = p(y_u \mid y_{-u}) = 1 / E[1 / p(y_u \mid \vartheta) \mid y],$$ an expectation over the full posterior. The posterior is taken as the Gaussian \(N(\tilde\vartheta, \Omega)\) of the fit, with the VB-corrected mean (the mode when vb = FALSE) and the Laplace covariance, and \(\ell_u\) is expanded to second order about \(\tilde\vartheta\), with score \(s_u\) and Hessian \(H_u\). The expectation is then a Gaussian integral: $$\log \mathrm{CPO}_u = \ell_u - \tfrac12 s_u^\top (\Omega^{-1} + H_u)^{-1} s_u + \tfrac12 \log |I + \Omega H_u|.$$ The same expansion gives the log pointwise predictive density $$\mathrm{lpd}_u = \log E[p(y_u \mid \vartheta) \mid y] = \ell_u + \tfrac12 s_u^\top (\Omega^{-1} - H_u)^{-1} s_u - \tfrac12 \log |I - \Omega H_u|$$ and the WAIC penalty \(p_{\mathrm{waic},u} = \mathrm{Var}[\ell_u(\vartheta)] = s_u^\top \Omega s_u + \tfrac12 \mathrm{tr}[(\Omega H_u)^2]\). Then \(\mathrm{elpd}_{\mathrm{loo}} = \sum_u \log \mathrm{CPO}_u\), \(p_{\mathrm{loo}} = \sum_u (\mathrm{lpd}_u - \log \mathrm{CPO}_u)\), \(\mathrm{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}} = \sum_u (\mathrm{lpd}_u - p_{\mathrm{waic},u})\), and looic and waic are \(-2\) times the elpd. Each standard error is \(\sqrt{n \, \mathrm{Var}}\) of the pointwise terms over the \(n\) units, as in the loo package.

The scores and Hessians come from finite differences of loglik along the principal axes of \(\Omega\), a hundredth of a posterior SD apart: \(m^2 + m + 1\) calls of loglik for \(m\) parameters, each returning every unit.

Existence and the leverage k. For each unit, the eigenvalues \(k\) of \(-\Omega H_u\) are the shares of the posterior precision the unit carries along its directions. The second-order \(\log \mathrm{CPO}_u\) exists only when every \(k < 1\): at \(k \ge 1\), the rest of the data and the prior cannot identify some combination of the parameters without the unit, and \(E[1 / p(y_u \mid \vartheta)]\) diverges. If any unit fails, every LOO estimate falls back to the first-order \(\log \mathrm{CPO}_u = \ell_u - \tfrac12 s_u^\top \Omega s_u\), with a warning naming the units, rather than mixing orders or dropping units. The largest \(k\) of each unit is reported as k, a measure of its influence. Likewise the second-order \(\mathrm{lpd}_u\) needs every \(k > -1\). Where that fails, WAIC falls back to first order, at which it equals the first-order LOO, and p_loo uses the first-order term for that unit.

The expansion rests on the Gaussian approximation of the posterior, as the VB correction does. A cross-check that uses the skew-normal marginals is Pareto-smoothed importance sampling on copula draws: loo::loo(sampling(fit, 4000, fun = loglik, ...)).

Silent fits

On a fit made with silent = TRUE, loo() and waic() print nothing and raise no warnings, their own or those of loglik; the warnings are kept in the result's warnings, and a fallback to first order shows in order and first_order_units.

Other objects

For any other object, loo() and waic() call the loo package's functions of the same name, if it is installed, so attaching inlavanilla after loo (or a package that uses it, such as rstan or brms) does not get in their way.

Comparing models

The results have the layout of the loo package's objects, so loo::loo_compare() compares fits to the same units. By hand, with d the difference of two fits' pointwise[, "elpd_loo"], the difference in elpd is sum(d) with standard error sqrt(length(d)) * sd(d).

References

Alhyari, M., Jamil, H., Montcho, H., & Rue, H. (2026). Deterministic leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation for multilevel Bayesian models (arXiv:2609.00670 [stat.ME]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.00670

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., & Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing, 27(5), 1413–1432. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4

Watanabe, S. (2010). Asymptotic equivalence of Bayes cross validation and widely applicable information criterion in singular learning theory. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11, 3571–3594. https://jmlr.org/papers/v11/watanabe10a.html

Examples

# Poisson counts: is a log-linear trend better than a constant rate?
y <- c(2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15)
time <- seq_along(y) - 5

loglik <- function(theta, time, y) {
  dpois(y, exp(theta[["a"]] + theta[["b"]] * time), log = TRUE)
}
logprior <- function(theta) sum(dnorm(theta, 0, 5, log = TRUE))
logpost <- function(theta, time, y) {
  sum(loglik(theta, time, y)) + logprior(theta)
}

fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, c(a = 0, b = 0), time = time, y = y)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 9 iterations [1ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.12σ [1ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [5ms]
loo(fit, loglik, time = time, y = y)
#> ── Leave-one-out cross-validation ─────────────────────────────── 9 units ──
#> 
#>           Estimate   SE
#> elpd_loo     -19.2  0.8
#> p_loo          0.6  0.2
#> looic         38.3  1.6
#> 
#> ✔ Second-order expansion for every unit. Largest leverage k = 0.49, for
#>   unit 9.
waic(fit, loglik, time = time, y = y)
#> ── WAIC ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 9 units ──
#> 
#>            Estimate   SE
#> elpd_waic     -19.1  0.8
#> p_waic          0.6  0.1
#> waic           38.3  1.6
#> 
#> ✔ Second-order expansion for every unit.
